title: State v. Gleason
description: Whether an instructional error that omits an essential element of a criminal offense requires automatic reversal under Section 5 of the Kansas Constitution Bill of Rights, or if it is subject to a harmless error analysis.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the Court of Appeals erred in reversing Gleason's conviction based on prosecutorial and cumulative error, and that the instructional error was harmless because the State rebutted the presumption of prejudice.
defendant_argument: Gleason argued that the Court of Appeals erred by applying a harmless error analysis to the instructional error, claiming it infringed on his constitutional right to a jury trial under Section 5 of the Kansas Constitution Bill of Rights, which he contended mandates automatic reversal for such errors.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' judgment, affirming the district court's conviction of Jason M. Gleason Sr., finding that the prosecutorial error was harmless and the instructional error, though presumed prejudicial, was rebutted by the State showing no actual prejudice to Gleason.

title: State v. Stubbs
description: Whether the criminal-use-of-weapons statute (K.S.A. 21-6301(a)(2)) is unconstitutionally vague because it lacks adequate enforcement standards, thereby impermissibly delegating legislative power, and whether there was sufficient evidence to support the defendant's interference-with-law-enforcement conviction.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that K.S.A. 21-6301(a)(2) provides adequate enforcement guidelines for possessing a 'dangerous knife' and that there was ample evidence Stubbs knowingly obstructed law enforcement.
defendant_argument: Stubbs argued that the criminal-use-of-weapons statute is unconstitutionally vague due to a lack of meaningful enforcement standards for 'dangerous knife,' and that the State failed to prove he knowingly obstructed law enforcement.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed both of Stubbs' convictions, ruling that while he had standing to bring the vagueness challenge, the statute was not unconstitutionally vague, and there was sufficient evidence for the interference-with-law-enforcement conviction.

title: State v. Phipps
description: Whether the completion of a criminal sentence renders an appeal moot, thereby extinguishing the court's jurisdiction to review the case, and whether "prudential exceptions" to mootness are constitutionally permissible in Kansas.
plaintiff_argument: Phipps argued that his case was not moot because the issues presented were of statewide importance and capable of repetition, and therefore, the court should review his challenge to his criminal history score.
defendant_argument: The State also argued that the case was not moot due to the statewide importance and repetitive nature of the issues, and that the Court of Appeals correctly affirmed Phipps' sentence based on Counterman.
decision_outcome: The court dismissed the appeal, ruling that Phipps' completion of his sentence rendered the case moot, and explicitly overruled prior caselaw that allowed for "prudential exceptions" to mootness, holding that once an issue is moot, jurisdiction is extinguished.

title: State v. Green
description: Whether the premeditated first-degree murder statute is unconstitutionally vague, whether the district court erred in excluding preliminary hearing testimony of an allegedly unavailable witness, and whether Green knowingly and intelligently waived his right to counsel at sentencing.
plaintiff_argument: The premeditated first-degree murder statute is unconstitutionally vague, the district court erred by not admitting a witness's preliminary hearing testimony based on counsel's statements of unavailability, and Green's waiver of counsel at sentencing was invalid due to an intervening event requiring a new colloquy.
defendant_argument: The premeditated first-degree murder statute is not unconstitutionally vague, Green failed to provide sufficient evidence to establish witness unavailability, and Green's initial waiver of counsel remained valid as no substantial change in circumstances occurred to require a new waiver at sentencing.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Green's convictions and sentence, finding no error in the district court's rulings on the premeditated first-degree murder statute's constitutionality, witness unavailability, or the waiver of counsel.

title: Kansas v. Harper
description: Whether the Kansas Department of Revenue (KDOR) is required to record an individual's biological sex at birth on driver's licenses, with the Attorney General arguing it is mandated by K.S.A. 77-207 and KDOR arguing it is not.
plaintiff_argument: The Attorney General (AG) argued that K.S.A. 77-207 applies to driver's licenses, requiring the KDOR to record biological sex at birth, and that "sex" and "gender" are synonymous. The AG also claimed KDOR's refusal to comply with the law constituted irreparable harm.
defendant_argument: The KDOR and Intervenors argued that K.S.A. 77-207 does not apply to driver's licenses, that "sex" and "gender" are not synonymous, and that the AG failed to demonstrate irreparable harm or a substantial likelihood of prevailing on the merits. They also contended that issuing driver's licenses involves discretion, making mandamus an improper remedy.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court denied the petition for review, allowing the Court of Appeals' decision to stand, which had reversed the district court's temporary injunction and remanded the case to a new judge.

title: Hodes & Nauser v. Kobach; Hodes & Nauser v. Stanek
description: Whether a series of state statutes and regulations relating to the licensure of abortion provider facilities are constitutional under section 1 of the Kansas Constitution Bill of Rights.
plaintiff_argument: The Challenged Laws infringe on a woman's fundamental right to personal autonomy, including the right to abortion, and do not survive strict scrutiny.
defendant_argument: The Challenged Laws are constitutional, do not infringe on the right to abortion, and serve compelling government interests in protecting maternal health and regulating the medical profession.
decision_outcome: The Kansas Supreme Court affirmed the district court's decision, striking down the Challenged Laws as unconstitutional and issuing a permanent injunction against their enforcement.

title: League of Women Voters of Kansas v. Schwab
description: Whether three new Kansas election laws, concerning false representation as an election official, signature verification for advance ballots, and restrictions on ballot collection, violate various provisions of the Kansas Constitution, including rights to free speech, the right to vote, equal protection, and due process.
plaintiff_argument: The League of Women Voters of Kansas and others argued that the false representation provision violates free speech, the signature verification requirement violates the right to vote, equal protection, and due process, and the ballot collection restriction violates the right to vote and free speech.
defendant_argument: Scott Schwab (Secretary of State) and Kris W. Kobach (Attorney General) argued that the laws are constitutional, with the false representation provision only regulating unprotected speech, the signature verification being a valid "proper proof" for electors, and ballot collection not constituting protected speech or expressive conduct.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the denial of a temporary injunction against the false representation provision, finding it likely unconstitutional as overbroad. It reversed the dismissal of claims against the signature verification requirement, remanding for review under equal protection and due process standards, but found the requirement itself a valid "proper proof" under Article 5. It affirmed the dismissal of claims against the ballot collection restriction, finding it neither an additional qualification on the right to vote nor an infringement on free speech.

title: City of Olathe v. City of Spring Hill
description: Whether an agreement between two cities to restrict future growth and annexation can legally bind subsequent city councils.
plaintiff_argument: Olathe argued the agreement was a valid, enforceable contract, authorized by state statutes, and necessary for planned development and avoiding chaotic land grabs.
defendant_argument: Spring Hill argued the agreement was unenforceable because an elected governing body cannot use its legislative power to constrain future governing bodies' policy decisions.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the district court's decision, ruling that the agreement between Olathe and Spring Hill was unenforceable as it attempted to bind future city councils on governmental policy decisions.

title: In re Schmidt
description: Whether the legislative reapportionment of state senatorial and representative districts, as contained in Substitute for Senate Bill 563, is valid under state and federal law, with the Attorney General arguing for its validity and an intervenor senator arguing against it due to procedural flaws and unconstitutional district boundaries.
plaintiff_argument: The Attorney General, as the petitioner, argued that the legislative enactment (Substitute for Senate Bill 563) is valid and contains no constitutional errors, having followed proper procedures and substantive requirements.
defendant_argument: Intervenor Senator Thomas Holland argued that Substitute for Senate Bill 563 is invalid due to procedural irregularities in its enactment and that the new district boundaries are unconstitutional, citing issues like lack of compactness, contiguity, and alleged political gerrymandering.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the legislative enactment, Substitute for Senate Bill 563, is valid, upholding the reapportionment maps for state senatorial and representative districts.

title: Rivera v. Schwab
description: Whether the Kansas Legislature's congressional redistricting map, "Ad Astra 2," violates the Kansas Constitution by engaging in partisan and racial gerrymandering and diluting minority votes.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the "Ad Astra 2" redistricting map constitutes unconstitutional partisan and racial gerrymandering and dilutes minority votes, violating various provisions of the Kansas Constitution, including equal protection, free speech, and voting rights.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the "Ad Astra 2" map is constitutional, that state courts lack jurisdiction to review partisan gerrymandering claims, and that plaintiffs failed to prove racial gerrymandering or vote dilution under the correct legal standards.
decision_outcome: The Kansas Supreme Court reversed the district court's judgment, finding that the plaintiffs did not establish that the "Ad Astra 2" redistricting map violated the Kansas Constitution, and lifted the injunction.

title: State v. Carr
description: Whether the Kansas capital sentencing scheme violates Section 1 of the Kansas Constitution Bill of Rights by infringing upon the right to life, which the plaintiff argues is absolute and nonforfeitable.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argues that Section 1 of the Kansas Constitution Bill of Rights guarantees an absolute, nonforfeitable right to life, which precludes the state from imposing capital punishment.
defendant_argument: The defendant argues that the natural right to life under Section 1 is forfeitable through criminal conduct, and thus the state's capital sentencing scheme does not unconstitutionally infringe upon this right.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Reginald Dexter Carr Jr.'s death sentence, concluding that the Kansas capital sentencing scheme does not violate Section 1 of the Kansas Constitution Bill of Rights.

title: State v. Carr
description: Whether Kansas' capital sentencing scheme violates Section 1 of the Kansas Constitution Bill of Rights, whether death qualification of jurors under K.S.A. 22-3410 violates Section 5 of the Kansas Constitution Bill of Rights, and whether various penalty-phase errors warrant reversal of Jonathan D. Carr's death sentence.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the capital sentencing scheme and death qualification process are constitutional, and that any alleged penalty-phase errors were harmless and do not warrant reversal of the death sentence.
defendant_argument: Jonathan D. Carr argued that the Kansas death penalty scheme violates his right to life under the Kansas Constitution Bill of Rights, that death qualification of jurors violates his right to a jury trial, and that numerous penalty-phase errors, including prosecutorial misconduct and improper jury instructions, cumulatively violated his rights and require reversal of his death sentence.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Jonathan D. Carr's death sentence, concluding he is not entitled to relief on the penalty-phase issues and that the evidence supports the aggravating circumstances outweighing mitigating circumstances.

title: State v. Brown
description: Whether the State's use of peremptory challenges was racially discriminatory, whether judicial fact-finding for criminal history violates the Kansas Constitution, and whether the criminal restitution scheme violates jury trial rights.
plaintiff_argument: Brown argued that the State's peremptory challenges were racially motivated, the Kansas Sentencing Guidelines Act (KSGA) violates Section 5 of the Kansas Constitution by allowing judges to determine criminal history for sentencing, and the criminal restitution scheme violates Section 5 and the Sixth Amendment by allowing judges to determine restitution damages.
defendant_argument: The State argued Brown failed to prove intentional discrimination in peremptory challenges, the KSGA does not violate Section 5, and the criminal restitution scheme does not violate the Sixth Amendment and its Section 5 issues are severable.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the denial of Brown's Batson challenge, affirmed the constitutionality of the KSGA's judicial fact-finding for criminal history, and affirmed the district court's restitution order after severing unconstitutional provisions, but remanded the case for resentencing due to an erroneous classification of Brown's prior Michigan juvenile adjudication for armed robbery.

title: State v. Arnett
description: Whether the Kansas criminal restitution statutes violate a defendant's right to a jury trial under the Sixth Amendment of the United States Constitution and section 5 of the Kansas Constitution Bill of Rights.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Taylor Arnett, argued that the restitution ordered against her violates her right to a jury trial under both the Sixth Amendment and section 5 of the Kansas Constitution Bill of Rights.
defendant_argument: The defendant, the State of Kansas, argued that criminal restitution does not violate the Sixth Amendment because it is not punishment, or if it is, it does not increase the statutory maximum, and that the Kansas restitution statutes do not violate section 5 of the Kansas Constitution Bill of Rights.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Court of Appeals' judgment, which affirmed the district court's restitution order, but found that certain Kansas restitution statutes violate section 5 of the Kansas Constitution Bill of Rights and severed the problematic portions.

title: State v. Robison
description: Whether the order of restitution in Robison's case violates either section 5 of the Kansas Constitution Bill of Rights or the Sixth Amendment of the United States Constitution, if not both, by allowing a judge to determine restitution amounts without a jury trial.
plaintiff_argument: Robison argued that the Kansas restitution statutes violate his right to a jury trial under both the Sixth Amendment and section 5 of the Kansas Constitution Bill of Rights, and that restitution should not be awarded to an insurance carrier.
defendant_argument: The State argued that criminal restitution is not punishment and does not trigger the right to a jury trial under the Sixth Amendment, and that criminal restitution is not a civil judgment under the Kansas Constitution.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's restitution order against Robison but found that certain Kansas criminal restitution statutes violated section 5 of the Kansas Constitution Bill of Rights and severed the unconstitutional portions that made criminal restitution equivalent to civil judgments without a jury trial.

title: State v. Albano
description: Whether the Kansas Sentencing Guidelines Act (KSGA) violates section 5 of the Kansas Constitution Bill of Rights by allowing courts, rather than juries, to make criminal history findings for sentencing purposes.
plaintiff_argument: Albano argued that the KSGA violates her right to trial by jury because it allows courts to make criminal history findings for sentencing, asserting that common law in 1859 required prior convictions that increased penalties to be proven to a jury beyond a reasonable doubt.
defendant_argument: The State argued that Kansas law traditionally distinguishes between the jury's role (guilt/innocence) and the court's role (punishment, including prior convictions), and therefore the KSGA's method for determining criminal history does not implicate the right to trial by jury.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the lower court's decision, ruling that the KSGA provisions allowing courts to make criminal history findings for sentencing purposes do not violate section 5 of the Kansas Constitution Bill of Rights.

title: Tillman v. Goodpasture
description: Whether a state statute abolishing 'wrongful birth' actions is constitutional, with plaintiffs arguing it violates their rights to a jury trial and legal remedy, and defendants arguing it is constitutional as wrongful birth was a new tort not protected by the constitution's adoption-era common law.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff parents allege their prenatal doctor negligently failed to inform them about serious fetal abnormalities, which would have led them to terminate the pregnancy, and argue that the statute abolishing 'wrongful birth' actions violates their constitutional rights to a jury trial and a legal remedy.
defendant_argument: The defendant, Dr. Goodpasture, and the intervenor, the Attorney General, argue that the statute is constitutional because 'wrongful birth' was a new cause of action recognized in 1990, not a common-law cause existing when the Kansas Constitution was adopted, and therefore is not protected by constitutional rights to a jury trial or a legal remedy.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the lower court's decision, ruling that the statute abolishing 'wrongful birth' actions is constitutional because it was a new tort not protected by the state constitution's adoption-era common law.
